Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
rehearse what to say before any interaction

Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I feel on guard even inside my own home
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.explanation: For a 42-year-old woman whose trauma type is stalking, helicopter or aircraft sounds are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The threat, memory, and maladaptive strategy items all describe hypervigilance, fragmented recall, and interpersonal avoidance consistent with stalking, but no other selected item suggests an aviation-related cue or context. This trigger appears clinically disconnected from the trauma type and from the strong Triggers→Threat / Triggers→Memory pattern in the formulation.

vignette:
Priya is a 42-year-old South Asian woman who works as a residential housekeeper, employed by a rotating roster of households in a mid-sized American city. She is married, the mother of two teenage children, and until approximately fourteen months ago she described herself as someone who had never given much thought to personal safety. That changed during the eight months she was stalked by a man who lived in the apartment building adjacent to one of her regular clients.

The stalking began gradually - a face she started recognising too often, a figure at the end of the street when she left work in the late afternoon. Over several months it escalated. He began appearing at the entrance of buildings she cleaned, waiting outside in a car she came to dread the sight of. On two occasions he followed her onto public transit. What crystallised the terror, and what Priya still cannot fully reconstruct in any ordered way, was an evening when he cornered her in a stairwell. He had been drinking - the smell of alcohol was dense and close - and what she remembers most viscerally, in the fragments she allows herself to approach, is the particular way he looked at her: a slow, deliberate scan of her body that she experienced as a physical act. He pressed her against the wall and she felt a sharp pain in her shoulder from the impact with the door frame. She does not know, even now, the full sequence of what happened next or how long it lasted. She screamed; a neighbour eventually opened a door. He left. She filed a police report, and he was subsequently issued a restraining order, but she has never felt that the danger conclusively ended.

In the months that followed, Priya's daily life reorganised itself around a logic of protection that has become exhausting to sustain. At work - moving through the private rooms of other people's homes - she encounters her triggers with a frequency that is almost impossible to manage. When a male employer lets his gaze linger on her in a way she reads as appraising, her body responds before her mind can intervene: her shoulder aches as though freshly struck, and sometimes she can taste the metallic dryness that was in her mouth that evening in the stairwell. The smell of alcohol - a glass of wine left on a counter, a recycling bin she is expected to empty - can stop her mid-movement in a way she finds deeply shaming. She has become meticulous about rehearsing every exchange before it happens, scripting her greetings, her requests, her refusals, because she has come to believe that any unplanned interaction could go wrong in ways she will not be able to manage.

At home, the vigilance does not ease. She checks the locks on the front door and every window before she can sit down, and then checks them again before bed, and sometimes once more at 2 a.m. when she wakes and cannot account for a sound. Silence in the house - the particular quiet that falls after her children have gone to school and her husband to work - fills her with a specific dread, as though stillness itself is the moment before something breaks through it. She has stopped seeing the two friends she was closest to before the stalking. She tells herself she is too tired, but what she is actually afraid of is that she will not be able to explain herself without telling the story, and the story, when she tries to locate it, comes apart in her hands - she cannot assemble it into something coherent, and she cannot hold it long enough to try before something in her pushes it away.

What worries her as much as her own suffering is what she imagines happening to her children and her husband. She tracks them by phone with an intensity she recognises as disproportionate but cannot moderate, certain that danger has not finished with her family.

Priya came to her first appointment after her husband found her re-checking the locks at three in the morning and gently told her he was frightened for her. She arrived rehearsed and composed. What she said she most wanted was to stop being afraid in her own home. What she seemed most afraid of was being asked to remember clearly what she has spent over a year trying not to fully know.
